title: Changing Social Hierarchies and Challenges to State Power
subject: AP World History
objectives: Explain how transoceanic empires created new, often race-based social hierarchies (c. 1450–1750)
Describe the casta system of colonial Latin America and the rise of new elites and identities
Analyze how subjugated and enslaved peoples challenged state power through rebellion, resistance, and the formation of new communities
Apply the Continuity and Change Over Time (CCOT) reasoning skill to the social transformations of the early-modern period

sections.heading: A Painting That Sorted People Into Boxes
sections.content:
In the 1700s, wealthy households across Spanish colonial Mexico hung a peculiar kind of painting on their walls. Called 'casta paintings,' they were arranged like charts: panel after panel showing a man of one ancestry, a woman of another, and their child — each combination carefully labeled with a special name. A Spanish father and an Indigenous mother produced a 'mestizo'; a Spanish father and an African mother a 'mulatto'; and the categories multiplied into dozens of finely graded labels. The paintings were, in effect, an attempt to draw a precise map of human worth based on ancestry and skin color, with people of pure Spanish descent at the top and everyone else slotted into ranked boxes below.

Those paintings capture something new and disturbing that the transoceanic empires created: social hierarchies organized explicitly around race. The joining of the hemispheres did not just move crops, silver, and diseases; it threw together Europeans, Indigenous Americans, and Africans in colonial societies that had never existed before, and the colonizers built rigid systems to rank and control these mixed populations. The casta system of Spanish America is the clearest example, but new racial and ethnic hierarchies emerged across the early-modern empires.

This is the final lesson of Unit 4, and it does double duty. First, it examines how the maritime empires reshaped society — creating new elites, new ethnic categories, and new bottom rungs defined by coerced labor and race. Second, it examines how the people crushed beneath these hierarchies fought back: the enslaved, the conquered, and the exploited challenged state power through rebellion, escape, and the building of new communities. And because this lesson closes a unit, it is also where we step back and practice an essential exam skill explicitly: Continuity and Change Over Time (CCOT) — the art of analyzing what transformed and what persisted across a stretch of history. The social world of 1750 was, in many ways, radically new; in other ways, it ran on very old patterns. Learning to say precisely which is which is the heart of historical thinking.

sections.heading: New Hierarchies: Race, the Casta System, and New Elites
sections.content:
The most striking social change of the period was the emergence of hierarchies built on race, especially in the Americas. In Spanish colonial society, a person's status was tied closely to ancestry, producing the casta system — an elaborate, legally and socially significant ranking of people by their European, Indigenous, and African descent. At the top stood the 'peninsulares' (those born in Spain), just below them the 'creoles' (criollos — people of European descent born in the Americas), then the various mixed-ancestry groups (mestizos of European-Indigenous descent, mulattoes of European-African descent, and many more), with Indigenous people and enslaved Africans at the bottom. Where you fell in this hierarchy shaped your legal rights, your job prospects, your taxes, and your social standing.

Notice that this was a genuinely new kind of social order. Earlier societies, of course, had steep hierarchies — nobles over peasants, free over enslaved (recall Unit 1). But the casta system tied status systematically to race and ancestry in a multi-continental colonial setting, an arrangement that had not existed before the transoceanic encounter. The Atlantic slave system reinforced it by making blackness and enslavement legally intertwined. Race as a structuring principle of society is, to a significant degree, an early-modern invention forged in these empires.

The period also produced new elites and resentments. The creoles are a crucial group to watch: often wealthy, educated, American-born landowners and merchants, they were nonetheless ranked below the peninsulares and shut out of the highest offices, which Spain reserved for those born in the mother country. This bred deep creole resentment of colonial rule — a resentment that, you will see in Unit 5, eventually helped ignite the Latin American independence revolutions. Meanwhile, across the empires, merchants and others enriched by the new global trade rose in wealth and influence, and some older elites declined. The social pyramid of 1750 had new occupants, new rules, and new tensions baked into it.

sections.question: The casta system of Spanish colonial America is best described as...
options: a system with no relationship to ancestry or race
a social hierarchy that ranked people according to their European, Indigenous, and African descent, with peninsulares at the top and Indigenous and enslaved people at the bottom
an economic policy for taxing trade between colonies
a religious order founded to convert Native Americans
sections.explanation: The casta system ranked colonial society by ancestry/race — peninsulares (Spain-born) and creoles at the top, mixed-ancestry groups in the middle, and Indigenous people and enslaved Africans at the bottom — shaping legal rights and social standing. It was fundamentally about ancestry (not unrelated to it), a social hierarchy rather than a tax policy or a religious order.

sections.heading: The Casta Hierarchy of Spanish America (Simplified)
rows: People born in Spain; held the highest offices
People of European descent born in the Americas; wealthy but barred from top posts
People of mixed European and Indigenous descent
People of mixed European and African descent
Subject to tribute and coerced labor (encomienda, mita)
Held as chattel property; status inherited and racialized

sections.heading: Fighting Back: Challenges to State Power
sections.content:
Wherever empires imposed coercion, people resisted — and the early-modern period is full of revolts and resistance that you should be able to cite as evidence. Resistance took many forms, from open rebellion to quieter strategies of survival and escape.

Enslaved Africans resisted the brutal Atlantic system constantly. Some rose in open revolt; many escaped. Across the Americas, escaped enslaved people formed independent settlements called maroon communities — in the mountains, jungles, and swamps of places like Brazil, Jamaica, and Suriname — where they built free societies and sometimes fought off colonial armies for decades. The most famous, Palmares in Brazil, survived for most of a century. These communities are powerful evidence that the enslaved were never passive victims but active agents resisting their bondage.

Indigenous peoples and other subjugated groups rebelled as well. The Pueblo Revolt of 1680 in New Mexico saw Indigenous peoples temporarily drive the Spanish out and reclaim their land and religion — one of the most successful Indigenous revolts in North American history. In Africa, leaders resisted European encroachment and the slave trade; Queen Nzinga of Ndongo and Matamba (in present-day Angola) skillfully fought and negotiated against Portuguese expansion for decades. And resistance was not only against European empires: peasants and others rebelled against the great land empires too. Cossack uprisings challenged Russian authority, and the Ottoman, Mughal, and Chinese states faced their own revolts. Across the early-modern world, the expansion of state power and coercion was met, again and again, by organized resistance from below. When the exam asks about 'challenges to state power' or how subjugated peoples responded to empire, these revolts and communities — maroons, Pueblo Revolt, Nzinga, Cossacks — are your concrete evidence.

Transoceanic empires created new race-based social hierarchies — above all the casta system of Spanish America, which ranked people by European, Indigenous, and African ancestry — while subjugated and enslaved peoples challenged state power through revolts and new communities (maroon settlements, the Pueblo Revolt of 1680, Queen Nzinga, Cossack uprisings).

sections.heading: Worked Example: A CCOT Analysis of Society, c. 1450 → c. 1750
sections.content:
Let's model the Continuity and Change Over Time skill on this unit's content, because CCOT questions ask exactly this: across a span of time, what changed and what stayed the same? A weak answer lists facts; a strong one sorts them into change and continuity and explains both. Take the prompt: 'Analyze continuities and changes in social hierarchies from c. 1450 to c. 1750.'

First, establish the baseline (c. 1450). Before the transoceanic age, societies across the world were already steeply hierarchical: rigid class and status divisions, hereditary elites (nobles, warrior aristocracies), patriarchal gender systems, and widespread coerced labor including various forms of slavery and serfdom. Hierarchy itself was old and nearly universal.

Now name the CHANGES by 1750. The joining of the hemispheres produced genuinely new social arrangements: race-based hierarchies like the casta system that ranked people by European/Indigenous/African ancestry; a new American-born creole elite resentful of peninsulares; and the rise of new merchant classes enriched by global trade. Atlantic chattel slavery created a uniquely racialized, hereditary form of bondage on an unprecedented scale. These are real transformations — the social map of 1750 contained categories of people that did not exist in 1450.

Now name the CONTINUITIES — and this is what separates a top answer. Beneath the novelty, deep patterns persisted: society remained steeply hierarchical and unequal; elites still dominated the masses; coerced labor remained the engine of economies (the form changed from, say, serfdom and older slaveries to chattel slavery and the encomienda, but the fact of forced labor continued); and patriarchy endured largely intact. So the precise CCOT claim is: 'From 1450 to 1750, the BASES and FORMS of social hierarchy changed dramatically — new race-based and creole/merchant categories emerged from global contact — even as the underlying REALITY of steep inequality, elite dominance, and coerced labor persisted.' That single sentence does what graders want: it holds change and continuity together and is specific about each. Memorize its shape — 'the form changed, the underlying pattern continued' — because it is the master move of CCOT writing.

sections.question: Maroon communities are significant evidence for which historical claim?
options: that enslaved people accepted their condition passively
that enslaved people actively resisted bondage, in this case by escaping and forming independent self-governing settlements that sometimes survived for decades
that slavery did not exist in the Americas
that European colonizers freed most enslaved people voluntarily
sections.explanation: Maroon communities were independent settlements formed by escaped enslaved people (e.g., Palmares in Brazil) who built free societies and sometimes resisted colonial armies for decades, demonstrating active resistance to bondage. They directly contradict the idea of passive acceptance, prove slavery's existence, and show freedom seized through escape, not granted by colonizers.

sections.heading: How to Write a Continuity and Change Over Time (CCOT) Answer

steps.title: Define the time span and establish the 'before'
steps.content: CCOT analysis lives in a specific period (here c. 1450–c. 1750). Start by sketching the situation at the beginning of the span — the baseline — so you have something to measure change against. You cannot show what changed without first establishing what it changed FROM. Anchor your span in the prompt's dates and stay inside them.

steps.title: Identify specific CHANGES and explain what caused them
steps.content: Name concrete transformations (e.g., new race-based casta hierarchies, the creole elite, Atlantic chattel slavery) and tie each to a cause (the joining of hemispheres, the silver/plantation economy, the slave trade). A change without a cause is just a fact; a change WITH a cause is analysis. Be specific — 'the casta system,' not 'society changed.'

steps.title: Identify specific CONTINUITIES — what persisted
steps.content: This is the step weak answers skip. Name what stayed the same across the span: steep social hierarchy, elite dominance, reliance on coerced labor, patriarchy. The best continuity point often shows that a deep PATTERN persisted even as its surface FORM changed (coerced labor continued, but shifted from serfdom/older slaveries to chattel slavery and the encomienda).

steps.title: Make a thesis that holds change and continuity together
steps.content: Combine both sides into one defensible claim, ideally with the 'form changed / pattern continued' structure: e.g., 'The bases of hierarchy changed (new racial and creole categories) even as steep inequality and coerced labor persisted.' Avoid the trap of writing only about change — CCOT explicitly rewards naming BOTH, and a thesis that does both, specifically, is what graders reward most.

sections.heading: On CCOT, Continuity Is Where Points Are Lost
sections.content: The single most common CCOT mistake is writing an essay that is all CHANGE and forgets CONTINUITY (or vice versa). Chief Reader reports repeatedly note that students describe how things changed but never state what stayed the same, leaving the 'continuity' half of the prompt unanswered and capping their score. Whenever you see 'continuity AND change,' literally make yourself write at least one strong, specific continuity (here: hierarchy itself, elite dominance, coerced labor, and patriarchy all persisted). Also avoid vague continuity like 'people still lived' — name a real historical pattern that endured. Pairing a specific change with a specific continuity, each explained, is the safe path to full credit.

sections.heading: Stock Resistance Evidence for 'Challenges to State Power'
sections.content: Prompts on resistance, rebellion, or 'challenges to state power' in this era are common, and a few memorized examples cover almost all of them: maroon communities / Palmares (escaped enslaved Africans), the Pueblo Revolt of 1680 (Indigenous revolt expelling the Spanish from New Mexico), Queen Nzinga (African resistance to Portuguese expansion), and Cossack and peasant uprisings (against Russian and other land empires). Having two or three of these ready, with a one-line description each, lets you supply specific evidence instantly instead of writing 'people resisted.'

sections.heading: Social Hierarchies, Resistance & CCOT Essentials
sections.content: NEW HIERARCHIES: race-based, especially the casta system of Spanish America — peninsulares (Spain-born) > creoles (European descent, American-born; resentful, barred from top posts) > mestizos (Euro-Indigenous) / mulattoes (Euro-African) > Indigenous and enslaved Africans. New merchant elites rise from global trade. RESISTANCE / challenges to state power: maroon communities (escaped enslaved; Palmares, Brazil), Pueblo Revolt 1680 (NM), Queen Nzinga (vs. Portugal in Angola), Cossack/peasant revolts (vs. Russia and land empires). CCOT SKILL: establish the 'before,' name specific CHANGES + causes, name specific CONTINUITIES (hierarchy, elite dominance, coerced labor, patriarchy all persisted), and write a thesis holding BOTH together — 'the form changed, the underlying pattern continued.'

sections.heading: Closing Unit 4: The World That 1750 Built
sections.content:
Step back and look at what Unit 4 has built, because it closes the first great chapter of the early-modern world and sets up everything after. In 1450, the Americas and Afro-Eurasia were separate worlds; by 1750 they were bound into a single, unequal, deeply interconnected global system. The technologies of Lesson 1 opened the oceans; the Columbian Exchange of Lesson 2 fused the hemispheres biologically and demographically; the maritime empires of Lesson 3 built the political-economic machinery — mercantilism, joint-stock companies, the silver circuit, and coerced labor — to extract wealth from that fused world; and this lesson has shown the human societies that resulted: new racial hierarchies, new elites, and the resistance of those crushed beneath them.

Now apply the CCOT lens to the whole unit, because that is the deep payoff. What changed by 1750 is enormous: a genuinely global economy, the demographic catastrophe of the Americas, the Atlantic slave system, race as a structuring principle of society, and the first tentative tilt of power toward Atlantic Europe. What continued is just as important to see: the world was still dominated by agrarian economies and steep hierarchies; the great Asian land empires (Unit 3) were still, in 1750, among the richest and most powerful states on earth; coerced labor and patriarchy endured as they had for millennia. Europe had inserted itself forcefully into the world but had not yet conquered or surpassed it.

That balance is precisely what is about to break. The tensions seeded here — creole resentment of colonial rule, Enlightenment ideas brewing in the Atlantic world, the staggering profits of the slave-and-plantation system, and the gradual accumulation of European commercial and naval power — are the kindling for the next period. In Units 5 and 6 you will watch revolutions and an industrial transformation ignite that kindling and finally tip the long-running contest decisively, reordering the entire globe. Unit 4 is the moment the modern world's foundations were poured. Hold its central CCOT insight — radical new global connections layered on top of stubbornly old patterns of hierarchy and coercion — as the lens through which the revolutions to come will make sense.
